member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Legacy.LegacyCipher
member.summary: The obfuscation scheme used by the VB6 application, provided for migration only.

remarks.para: modMain.bas defined a matched pair:
remarks.code: Function EncryptIt(s As String, Crack As Integer) As String For i = 1 To Len(s) Z = Z + Chr(Asc(Mid(s, i, 1)) + Crack) Next i End Function
remarks.para: It is a Caesar shift, called throughout the application with a shift of 11. It is not encryption and not a hash: every stored password is trivially recoverable, and the shift is a literal in the source.

This class exists so the extract-transform-load can read legacy values. Nothing in the application protects anything with it. Passwords migrate to PBKDF2 through ASP.NET Core Identity, or to a forced reset — see docs/03-Database-Migration-Plan.md §6.

member.param: The shift; the legacy application always used 11.

member.remarks: Provided only so migration tooling can match against values still stored in the legacy databases. Never use it to store anything.

member.name: F:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Legacy.LegacyCipher.DetectionIsUndecidable
member.summary: Whether a stored value can be told apart from its shifted form automatically.

remarks.para: It cannot, and this method documents why rather than pretending otherwise. Shifting jdoe by 11 gives uozp — still lowercase letters, still a plausible user name. Shifting SOFT2O12 gives ^ZQ_=Z<=, which is unusual but entirely printable. No character-class test separates the two reliably.

This matters because the VB6 source is inconsistent about whether user names are stored shifted: modSub.addUserName decrypts them when filling a combo box, modPermission.prcAddUserName has that same call commented out, frmCreateUser shifts the name to search for it, and frmUserLogIn compares the typed name against the stored value unshifted. Those four cannot all be right.

The extract-transform-load therefore resolves it empirically, once per legacy database: take an account whose sign-in name is known, compare it against both interpretations of the stored value, and apply whichever matches to every row in that database. Guessing per row would risk silently corrupting user names.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Legacy.LegacyPermissionMap
member.summary: Translates legacy menu grants into permissions.

remarks.para: The VB6 application stored one row per user per menu item across Sys_User_MM, Sys_User_MS and Sys_User_MSS, keyed by the VB menu control's name. This map is how a migrated user keeps the access they had.

The mapping is coarser in one direction and finer in another. Coarser, because a single menu item such as mnuNewSupplier covers viewing, creating, editing and deleting — the legacy application had no concept of operation-level permission. Finer, because permissions are checked on endpoints rather than menus, so a granted menu no longer implies its siblings are reachable.

member.name: F:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Legacy.LegacyPermissionMap.LeakedByInvisibleAll
member.summary: Menu items that prcMenuInvisibleAll leaves visible to every non-administrator.

remarks.para: prcMenuInvisibleAll exists to hide every menu before per-user grants selectively restore them. Eleven of its assignments set .Visible = True instead, including Purchase Order entry, MRR entry, the user-to-company permission screen and the data-lock screen. Each becomes reachable as soon as its parent menu is granted, whatever the user's own grant for the item says.

These are listed so the migration does not reproduce the exposure. A user's permissions are built from their recorded grants only; access they had solely through this defect is not carried over, and the extract-transform-load reports anyone affected.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Persistence.DocumentNumberAllocator
member.summary: Allocates document numbers under a row lock, so concurrent callers queue rather than collide.

remarks.para: This is the replacement for the legacy fncNewID2 in ModBill.bas:
remarks.code: Mysql = "Select Max(SupplierID) AS NewID From Supplier_Information;" If IsNull(RS(0).Value) Then fncNewID2 = 1 Else fncNewID2 = RS(0).Value + 1
remarks.para: That read was unlocked and untransacted, so two operators saving at the same moment both read the same maximum and both wrote the same number. The desktop application's low concurrency hid the defect; a web application would not.
Here the counter row is read with UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK inside a transaction, so the second caller blocks until the first commits. See docs/03-Database-Migration-Plan.md §3.3.

member.name: M:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Persistence.DocumentNumberAllocator.LoadLockedSequenceAsync(System.Int32,SupplyChain.Domain.Enums.DocumentType,System.Int32,System.Threading.CancellationToken)
member.summary: Reads the counter row with an update lock held to the end of the transaction.
member.remarks: Raw SQL is used because EF Core has no provider-agnostic way to express a locking hint. Parameters are passed through interpolation, which EF converts into instances rather than string concatenation — the legacy code built every statement by concatenation, which is why the application was comprehensively SQL-injectable.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Persistence.DocumentNumberGenerator
member.summary: Issues document numbers from a locked sequence row.

remarks.para: Replaces fncNewID, fncNewID2 and fncNewID3 in the legacy modules, which allocated with MAX(id) + 1 across roughly thirty entity types, with no lock and no transaction. Two concurrent saves produced the same number.

On SQL Server the sequence row is read WITH (UPDLOCK, HOLDLOCK), so a second caller blocks until the first commits. Other providers fall back to a tracked read: the unique index on company, type and year still prevents duplicates, and the write fails rather than silently duplicating.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Persistence.Interceptors.AuditableEntityInterceptor

remarks.para: Replaces several hundred lines of hand-written assignment in the VB6 forms. Nearly every INSERT in the legacy codebase carried USERID, PCName, EntryDate and EntryTime spelled out by hand — with inconsistent casing, occasionally in a different column order, and sometimes omitted altogether.
Centralising it here means audit data cannot be forgotten, and the legacy inconsistency disappears by construction.

member.name: T:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Reporting.StatementQueryFilters
member.summary: Filters shared by the statement reports.

remarks.para: frmrptPartyStatement.frm contained a hundred SQL statements in 752 lines — the densest query logic in the legacy application. Almost all of that volume came from writing out every combination of party, date basis, transaction type and company scope as its own literal string, then repeating the set once per company database.
Composing predicates instead means each filter is written once, and adding one does not multiply the others.

member.name: M:SupplyChain.Infrastructure.Reporting.StatementQueryFilters.ApplyScope(System.Linq.IQueryable{SupplyChain.Domain.Entities.Statements.CashCreditStatement},System.Boolean)
member.remarks: Call this before any join. IgnoreQueryFilters applies to the whole query rather than the operand it is called on, so calling it later — or on a joined set that needs no filtering — silently disables tenant isolation for everything. That happened in Wave 3 and one company's rows appeared in another's report.

member.summary: Applies the party, date, and type filters, each only when supplied.

remarks.para: Replaces four VB6 forms and four Crystal report files. All four ran the same query against viewStatement_Cash_Credit and differed only in which column the WHERE clause filtered on; frmrptTransactionWiseReport alone contained an eight-branch nested If building one of eight nearly identical SQL strings.
Here the filters compose. Each is applied only when supplied, so the eight branches collapse into a query built once.
